Alright, the project is shaping up nicely. I've already scaffolded the server side (index.js, realtime.js) and the basic front‑end assets (HTML, CSS, API wrapper, 2D avatar renderer). The next major component is the 3D engine, specifically the physics and character controller that will drive player movement in the world built from the primitive parts.

Looking at the files I've added so far in the `public/js/engine` folder, I have `world.js` which sets up a three.js scene, defines the set of solid part types, and provides a `setupScene` function. The world builder also likely includes utilities for handling part geometry (e.g., `partCenter`) and a map of parts. The next logical piece is a physics module that will consume those world parts and implement an axis‑aligned bounding box (AABB) character controller, similar to what Roblox does for its classic “blocky” physics.

I need to decide what this module should expose. The rest of the client code will need to create a controller instance, pass in the world object (so it can query parts), and then on each animation frame call a `step(dt, input)` method. It should also expose some configuration constants (player dimensions, step height) and perhaps some events (e.g., `onJump`). The controller will need to track position, velocity, grounded state, water detection, speed pads, and a list of “touching” special parts (coins, checkpoints, etc.) for later handling.

I’ll start by importing THREE because I’ll use `THREE.Vector3` for positions and velocities, and also import the `SOLID_TYPES` set from `world.js` to know which parts are solid for collision. Then define a constant `PLAYER` with half‑width and half‑height (matching typical Roblox avatar dimensions). A `STEP_HEIGHT` constant will control auto‑stepping.

The class `CharacterController` will take a `world` reference and a `config` object (holding gravity, walk speed, jump power). In the constructor I’ll initialise:
- `this.world = world;`
- `this.config = config;`
- `this.pos = new THREE.Vector3(0, 6, 0);` – start the player a bit above ground.
- `this.vel = new THREE.Vector3();`
- `this.grounded = false;`
- `this.groundPart = null;`
- `this.groundPrev = new THREE.Vector3();` – to track mover platforms.
- `this.inWater = false;`
- `this.onSpeedPad = false;`
- `this.touching = [];` – for special parts each frame.

A `teleport(v)` helper will directly set position and zero velocity, resetting ground state – useful for respawns.

Collision detection needs a method to collect nearby solid parts. I'll implement `_solids()` that iterates over `this.world.parts.values()`, filters by `SOLID_TYPES`, computes each part’s center via `this.world.partCenter(part, c)`, and does a cheap distance check (±8 units) to prune far parts. It then returns an array of objects with the part reference and pre‑computed min/max extents on each axis.

I also need a generic overlap test `_overlaps(b, px, py, pz, pad=0)` that checks whether the player’s AABB (centered at (px,py,pz) with half‑sizes from `PLAYER`) overlaps a given bounding box `b`, optionally expanded by `pad` (used for detecting proximity to coins etc.).

The core `step(dt, input)` method will:
1. Clamp `dt` to a max of 0.05 to keep the simulation stable.
2. Compute movement speed, applying a multiplier if the player is on a speed pad.
3. Convert input’s camera‑relative `moveX`/`moveZ` into world‑space dx/dz using yaw.
4. Normalize the direction if its length exceeds 1.
5. Apply mover‑carry logic: if the player is standing on a moving platform (`groundPart.type === 'mover'`), compute the platform’s delta since last frame (`groundPrev`) and add it to the player position.
6. Apply gravity and input to velocity. In water, gravity is reduced, vertical velocity is damped, and horizontal speed is scaled down. Jumping in water adds a small upward boost. Otherwise, apply normal gravity, set horizontal velocity to `dx * walk` etc., and handle jumping when grounded.
7. Clamp vertical velocity to a terminal fall speed of -80.
8. Gather solid candidates via `_solids()`, reset grounded flags, then resolve Y movement: add `vel.y * dt` to `pos.y`, iterate over solids, and if overlapping, push the player out either upward (landing) or downward (head hit). When landing, set `grounded = true` and record `groundPart`.
9. Resolve X and Z movement separately via a helper `_moveAxis(solids, axis, delta)`. This helper will move the player along one axis, check for overlaps, attempt auto‑step (if grounded and the step height is within `STEP_HEIGHT`), and otherwise push the player back to the edge of the colliding box.
10. After movement, update `groundPrev` if the new ground part is a mover.
11. Finally, detect special part touches: reset `touching`, `inWater`, `onSpeedPad`; iterate over all world parts, skip normal solids, compute a padded bounding box (larger for coins), and if overlapping, set the appropriate flags or push the part onto `touching`. Also include the ground part if it’s a special type (bounce, speed, tele, checkpoint, goal, kill).

The `_moveAxis` helper needs to handle the auto‑step logic: when moving horizontally and grounded, check if the colliding block’s top is within `STEP_HEIGHT` above the player’s current Y; if so, verify there’s clearance at that stepped height (by checking other solids). If clear, raise the player to the step height and continue. If stepping isn’t possible, clamp the player’s position to the side of the block.

All of this matches the typical Roblox‑style physics and will integrate cleanly with the rest of the engine. The code is now ready to be written to `public/js/engine/physics.js`. I’ll construct the file content exactly as outlined, making sure to include all imports, constants, class definition, and methods with proper formatting and comments.

Now I’ll issue the write tool call with the full file content.
